Photograph: Supplied UK news Pakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’ Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester Shah Meer Baloch and Rajeev Syal Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.41 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A grooming gang suspect released on bail in the UK and then re-elected as an MP in Pakistan has reportedly declined to say when he would return to face rape charges. The Guardian disclosed that Rukhsar Ahmed, a former Pakistan state minister, was arrested at Manchester airport in July 2024 on suspicion of raping and trafficking at least two underage girls from care homes in the city’s Rusholme area during the 1990s. He was released on bail and flew to Pakistan nearly two months ago, missing an appointment at a police station after telling officers he was too unwell to fly back to the UK. He was elected an MP for prime minister Shehbaz Sharif’s centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz party days later. He did not respond to requests for a comment when approached by the Guardian last week. View image in fullscreen Rukhsar Ahmed. Photograph: Supplied It emerged on Sunday that Ahmed, 61, had been located in his office in Khari Sharif, a village in Mirpur district. According to the Mail on Sunday, he told a reporter he would fly back to Britain to meet his bail conditions, but declined to give a date. “Everything is with my legal team in Manchester and London, they told me I can’t discuss this,” he told the newspaper. “What they done, this media in the United Kingdom and Europe, is out of order. I have not been convicted of anything nor charged for anything, so what is going on? I don’t want to discuss it, because if I discuss it, things may go wrong.” Asked directly whether he had raped two underage girls, he refused to answer, telling the reporter: “You are doing wrong now, I told you not to talk to me like this … please don’t talk to me like this, I told you I have nothing to do with it, OK.” Ahmed published a statement on his Facebook account on Friday. It read: “I categorically deny all the allegations against me and will address these matters through the appropriate forums. On legal advice, I will not comment further while these matters remain ongoing.” Ahmed was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021. The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024. Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area, where he lived for many years. According to the report, he received a string of visitors in his office. He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile. The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s. He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him. The Guardian has approached Ahmed for comment again. Richard Scorer, the head of abuse law at Slater and Gordon who has acted in many Manchester grooming gang cases said: “Rusholme has regularly featured in grooming gang investigations over the past 30 years, with many cases involving allegations of children being abused in and around the area. “Not all of those allegations have been adequately investigated. I hope that a comprehensive investigation is taking place here”. Photograph: Justin Lane/EPA Trump-Russia investigation Trump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against president Joe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 election Aram Roston and agencies Thu 10 Sep 2026 18.19 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A longtime ally of Donald Trump resigned from his post leading a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president. “Sometimes people want things done faster and that’s all you can do,” Joe diGenova said on Thursday. He appeared to be referring to concerns among other Trump loyalists that the president’s retribution cases were not moving quickly enough. “The bottom line is it takes a long time to make good cases, and you simply have to work at it,” he added. “All you can do is do the best you can under the circumstances.” The departure injects instant tumult into an investigation targeting former government officials who have investigated Trump over the last decade, including in connection with Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and his retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida. The Florida-based investigation has proceeded in fits and starts since its inception a year ago, with its contours loosely defined, though it had shown recent signs of activity with new subpoenas demanding testimony before a federal grand jury. While retribution by the justice department against Trump’s perceived adversaries has been one of the president’s highest priorities, diGenova’s comments hint at internal dissent and disagreement over the cases. He declined to say exactly why he resigned. “I’m not going to make any comments about indictments or anything else,” diGenova said. “When you’ve been a prosecutor as long as I have you know how to make cases, and it takes time. And that’s just part of the process. And sometimes that works out, and sometimes it doesn’t.” During the first Trump administration , diGenova was a legal adviser to John Solomon, a conservative journalist who has played an official role in White House efforts to push the conspiracy allegations. In an interview later with the New York Post, diGenova responded to criticism of his management of the investigation by saying: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin? Read more A spokesperson for the justice department did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The 81-year-old diGenova served as the US attorney for the District of Columbia during the Reagan administration. A close Trump ally, he was brought back to the justice department in April and given responsibility for an investigation aimed at trying to establish a conspiracy against Trump. DiGenova had previously asked the then US attorney general, Pam Bondi, to appoint him to the job and had openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy. But five months later, no charges have been brought, and it remains unclear whether any will be, or what information has been gathered to support any basis for the idea of a plot against Trump by the government officials who investigated him. The investigation has focused intensely on one of Trump’s chief grievances: a US intelligence community assessment that Russia had interfered on his behalf in the 2016 presidential election. The president and some of his supporters have long decried that conclusion as a “deep state” plot to undermine the legitimacy of his win. Multiple government investigations, including by a justice department special counsel and by the department’s own inspector general, have concluded that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion to help get Trump elected. The year-long investigation had proceeded in fits and starts well before diGenova’s appointment, which was announced soon after a career national security prosecutor who had been playing a key role in the investigation was replaced on the inquiry after raising doubts about its legal viability. Photograph: Joel Bissell/Kalamazoo Gazette/AP Michigan Federal court rejects Trump order keeping Michigan coal plant open A federal court is declaring that the energy department exceeded its authority when it forced a Michigan power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date Associated Press Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In a defeat for the Trump administration , a federal court on Friday ruled that the energy department exceeded its authority when it forced a Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date last year. Energy secretary Chris Wright had said the 64-year-old JH Campbell Generating Plant was needed to ensure reliable electricity in the region, and he used emergency powers to keep it operating. Environmental groups and three states – Michigan , Illinois and Minnesota – went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plant online. The US court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law. The section of the Federal Power Act that allows emergency orders “is essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop”, appeals court judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel. By reversing the Campbell plant’s “long and carefully planned retirement … the results are disruptive,” Pillard wrote. There was “no ‘emergency’ within the meaning” of the statute, she added. The Michigan case is one of several legal disputes that have emerged across the country as the Trump administration uses emergency powers to force a half-dozen coal-fired plants from closing. The orders, which also apply to plants in Indiana, Colorado, Florida and Washington state, are raising ratepayer bills and adding air and water pollution that could have been avoided, critics say. An oil and gas plant in Pennsylvania was also ordered to keep its turbines running as a hedge against electricity shortages in the mid-Atlantic grid. Keeping the Michigan plant open beyond its May 2025 retirement has cost about $259m so far, according to new financial filings. Those losses will probably be paid by families and businesses in the midwest, opponents of the order say. Ted Kelly, US clean energy director at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the court ruling rejected the Trump administration’s nationwide effort to force “unreliable, ageing coal plants that are bleeding money and polluting communities to stay online”. The energy department’s “unlawful actions attempted to make families and businesses in the midwest wastefully pay hundreds of millions of dollars for a coal plant that should have been shut down over a year ago,” Kelly said Friday. The Campbell plant and other ageing sites are “incredibly expensive, dangerous to our health and break down frequently”, he said. Sanjay Narayan, a lawyer for the Sierra Club, called the ruling a victory for families across the midwest who are “paying to keep this old, expensive and dirty power plant online”. The Trump administration “has been pulling out all the stops to try to bolster dirty and expensive fossil fuels at public expense. This reckless agenda will not succeed,” Narayan said. “We will continue to fight back against the other illegal extensions across the country.” The energy department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP Aukus Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, Peter Briggs says personnel is just one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Narelle Towie in Perth Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal , a retired admiral has warned. As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program. We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up? Read more As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete. The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class. The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline. View image in fullscreen Captain Justin Reeves talks to the media on USS Colorado at HMAS Stirling in Perth. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP “Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said. “By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.” But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats. Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia? Read more “We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said. “You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.” Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels. The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK. View image in fullscreen Crew members on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP “The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said. The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements. The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track. Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians. After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet. From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling. Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”. Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated. Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment. USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”. Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons. It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port. View image in fullscreen Sleeping quarters on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials. Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties. In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms. Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”. Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said. “Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.” Explore more on these topics Aukus Australian military US military news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
